name: 1Password breach
tile_line: Customer names and emails taken. Vaults not affected.
tldr: An attacker used an employee's GitHub account to push malicious code to 1Password's backend and copied names, emails and other account data for a subset of customers (no number given). Vaults weren't affected. No account changes needed; watch for phishing.
summary: The records also held account and user IDs, creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password parameters, the tokens in certain invitation, provisioning and recovery emails, and other non-secret metadata; the attacker also copied private source code and reached 1Password's CI/CD system, which holds infrastructure secrets. 1Password says the SRP parameters "cannot be used to access your account". It doesn't say how many customers are in the subset, when the attacker first got in, or who did it.

root_cause.text: An employee's corporate GitHub account. 1Password lists revoking "the stolen token" among its fixes, but doesn't say what kind of token it was, how the account was taken over, or when. With it the attacker reached source code and pushed malicious code to backend services, which downloaded the customer records.

timeline.text: 1Password begins investigating signs that an attacker got into an employee's corporate GitHub account.

1Password publishes its incident post. By then it had disabled the GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, restored clean versions of the affected service, rotated or revoked internal credentials that may have been exposed and lengthened the codes in invitation and recovery emails. It says it will keep the post current.

affected.label: You have a 1Password account
affected.text: The attacker downloaded account records for "a subset" of users. 1Password gives no number and doesn't say how to tell whether you're in it. It says vaults, the items in them, the keys that protect them, account recovery keys, and its apps and browser extensions weren't affected, and that it doesn't store your account password or Secret Key. It notified the small number of users with a provisioning invite or account recovery in progress, but doesn't say whether it is telling the rest of the subset.

do.label: No account changes needed
do.text: 1Password says you don't need to update anything in your account, and that it found no internal sign of account takeovers or of anyone using the exposed provisioning tokens.

do.label: Watch for phishing
do.text: Be wary of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations or account recovery you didn't start. 1Password says it will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key: only enter them in the official app or on its official website, opened or typed yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser. Report anything suspicious to `support@1password.com`. Our advice: since 1Password says no account changes are needed, treat any message about this incident that asks you to sign in, enter your Secret Key, accept an invitation or start an account recovery as phishing, and open 1Password yourself instead of following links in the message.

do.label: If 1Password notified you
do.text: That notice went to users with a provisioning invite (SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning) or account recovery in progress. The copied email token only works together with an SSO sign-in or the code emailed to you, and 1Password lengthened that code from six digits to ten letters and numbers. 1Password doesn't say whether the copied email tokens were cancelled or what these users should do; our advice is to complete only an invitation or recovery you started yourself.

versions_skip: 1Password's backend is a hosted service and 1Password names no software flaw: the attacker used an employee's GitHub account. There's nothing for users to install.
